---
title: "Beyond the Location: Which, How Sure, and What If"
author: "Youzhi Yu<br><span style='font-size:85%;'>University of Chicago</span>"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", dpi = 72,
                      fig.width = 8, fig.height = 3.2, message = FALSE,
                      warning = FALSE)
library(ggchangepoint)
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_ggcpt())
has_anomaly <- requireNamespace("anomaly", quietly = TRUE)
```

A detector answers *where*. Every applied field then asks the same few
questions: which of the measured quantities changed, how sure the
location is, what the series would have done otherwise, whether the
change was a jump at all, and, with many series, which ones changed. This
page answers each with one function, on data where the answer is known.

## Which coordinates changed

Testing each sensor at the detected changepoint is the obvious answer and
an invalid one: the location was chosen where the evidence across all of
them peaks, so an unchanged sensor is tested at the split most favourable
to it. `cpt_attribute()` scores each coordinate by the maximum of a rank
statistic over every split instead (ARM, Peng et al. 2026), so the
certificate cannot depend on how the location was found.

```{r attribute}
set.seed(1)
n <- 200
X <- matrix(rnorm(n * 8), n, 8, dimnames = list(NULL, paste0("sensor", 1:8)))
X[101:n, 3] <- X[101:n, 3] + 1.2      # a shift in sensor3
X[101:n, 6] <- X[101:n, 6] * 2.5      # a scale change in sensor6
fit_mv <- cpt_detect(X, method = "ecp")
att <- cpt_attribute(fit_mv, B = 499, seed = 1)
att
```

```{r attribute-plot, fig.height = 3.6, fig.alt = "Coordinate by changepoint map with the two certified sensors outlined"}
autoplot(att)
```

The two changed sensors are certified, each with its type, and the six
that did not change are left alone. Measured on the calibration design,
the family-wise error over the unchanged coordinates is:

```{r attribute-cal}
cal <- cpt_calibration
cal[grepl("cpt_attribute", cal$call), c("setting", "nominal", "realised", "mcse")]
```

## How sure is the location, with no model

`cpt_confint(method = "conformal")` returns a set of locations that holds
the true one with probability at least the level, for any distribution of
the noise, provided the observations within each segment are exchangeable
(Hore and Ramdas 2026). Here on heavy-tailed noise, where a Gaussian
interval has no footing:

```{r conformal}
set.seed(2)
y <- c(rt(150, df = 3), rt(150, df = 3) + 1.5)
fit <- cpt_detect(y, method = "pelt")
ci <- cpt_confint(fit, method = "conformal", B = 199, seed = 1)
ci
```

```{r conformal-profile, fig.alt = "Conformal p-value of every candidate location, with the 0.05 line"}
prof <- attr(ci, "profile")
ggplot(prof, aes(position, p_value)) +
  geom_col(width = 1, fill = "#5e3c99") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(120, 180)) +
  labs(x = "Candidate location", y = "Conformal p-value")
```

The coverage, measured on the calibration design and against the
bootstrap:

```{r conformal-cal}
cal[grepl("location", cal$guarantee) & grepl("conformal|bootstrap", cal$call),
    c("call", "nominal", "realised", "mcse")]
```

`cpt_confint_coverage()` runs the same study for your own length, jump and
noise.

## What would have happened

`cpt_counterfactual()` carries the segment before each change forward with
its own model, with a prediction band, and the gap is the effect in the
data's units: the figure interrupted-time-series studies report.

```{r counterfactual, fig.alt = "Nile flow with the pre-1898 level carried forward as a dashed counterfactual"}
nile <- cpt_detect(Nile, method = "amoc", change_in = "meanvar")
cf <- cpt_counterfactual(nile)
glance(cf)
autoplot(cf)
```

## Was it a jump?

Every engine looks for a jump, and given a transition that took thirty
observations it reports one confidently placed changepoint in the middle.
`cpt_abruptness()` fits a step and a ramp at each changepoint and reports
the transition width with an interval:

```{r abruptness, fig.alt = "A gradual transition with the fitted step and the fitted ramp"}
sim <- cpt_simulate(300, changepoints = 150, params = c(0, 3),
                    transition = 40, seed = 3)
ab <- cpt_abruptness(cpt_detect(sim$value, method = "pelt"))
ab
autoplot(ab)
```

## A change that comes back

An outbreak that subsides or a fault that is repaired is a stretch away
from a baseline, not a new regime. CAPA models exactly that, and reports
the stretches and the single outliers:

```{r capa, eval = has_anomaly, fig.alt = "Series with an anomalous stretch shaded and a point anomaly ringed"}
set.seed(4)
z <- c(rnorm(150), rnorm(40, 2.5), rnorm(150))
z[60] <- 7
ep <- cpt_detect(z, method = "capa")
cpt_regions(ep)
autoplot(ep)
```

## How many changes, and which series

`cpt_k_weights()` turns the criterion curve of `cpt_select()` into weights
over the number of changes, and averages the candidate segmentations into a
probability at each location:

```{r k-weights, fig.alt = "Weights over the number of changepoints"}
set.seed(5)
w <- cpt_k_weights(cpt_select(c(rnorm(100), rnorm(100, 0.8), rnorm(100)),
                              criterion = "bic", k_max = 6))
w
autoplot(w)
```

And for a panel, `cpt_screen()` tests every series for a change anywhere
and controls the false discovery rate across them:

```{r screen, fig.alt = "Sorted p-values of 60 series against the Benjamini-Hochberg line"}
set.seed(6)
panel <- c(lapply(1:52, function(i) rnorm(120)),
           lapply(1:8, function(i) c(rnorm(60), rnorm(60, 1.2))))
names(panel) <- paste0("store", 1:60)
sc <- cpt_screen(panel)
glance(sc)
autoplot(sc)
```
